description: The Federal National Mortgage Association, or Fannie Mae, is a major player in the secondary mortgage market. The company buys housing loans from issuers and either holds them or packages them into securities it sells to investors. Founded in 1938 as part of the New Deal, Fannie Mae became a shareholder-owned corporation in 1968. In 2008, in the wake of the Global Financial Crisis and a nationwide crash in housing values, Fannie Mae was delisted from the New York Stock Exchange and entered government conservatorship. It returned to profitability in 2012.

rankings.title: Fortune 500
rankings.itemDescription:
The government-backed mortgage financing giant moved up five spots on this year’s list, bringing in $122 billion in revenue. But a slowing housing market sharply reduced the number of mortgages that Fannie Mae purchased, securitized, and otherwise guaranteed.

  • For its 2022 fiscal year, the company said, it supported $684 billion worth of housing activity, down about 50% from 2021. That included acquiring about 1,151,000 single-family mortgages (more than 45% of which went to first-time homebuyers) and 886,000 single-family-home refinancing loans.

  • Fannie Mae also reported financing approximately 598,000 units of rental housing in 2022, a majority of which it says were affordable to households earning at or below 120% of area median income.

rankings.title: Fortune 500
rankings.itemDescription: The crazy pandemic-era housing price boom might not have been possible without Fannie Mae. The government-backed enterprise doesn’t issue mortgages directly, but it purchases, securitizes, and guarantees loans made by other lenders, which attracts investors and helps keep the mortgage market liquid. Fannie Mae reported in February that it had acquired 1.4 million single-family home loans and 3.3 million refinanced mortgages in 2021, backing more than $450 billion worth of home purchases.

rankings.title: Fortune Global 500
rankings.itemDescription: As a government-sponsored enterprise, Fannie Mae plays a critical role in underpinning the U.S. housing market—and, in turn, the American economy at large. The pandemic only highlighted that importance; Fannie provided a record $1.4 trillion in liquidity to the single- and multifamily mortgage markets in 2020, allowing homeowners to take advantage of historically low interest rates to purchase homes at a breakneck pace, and to refinance 3.4 million loans across the U.S. last year. Despite the surprising strength in those markets, Fannie’s 2020 results were hindered by the pandemic; revenues fell 11.5% from the previous year, while profits slipped nearly 17%.

rankings.title: Fortune Global 500
rankings.itemDescription: Government–backed Fannie Mae remains a vital cog in the U.S. housing market. Fannie provided more than $650 billion in liquidity to the residential mortgage market last year by purchasing or securitizing the loans behind more than 3 million home purchases, re-financings, and rentals. In addition to financing roughly one in four single-family mortgages in the U.S., the company backed $70 billion in multifamily financing in 2019, with the overwhelming bulk of that supporting affordable-housing units. Revenues ticked up 1% last year; profits, however, slid 11%.
